tagline: Twenty-eight roads follow a creek valley shaped by mills and crossings
intro: Red Clay Scenic Byway follows the contours of a creek watershed through flood plains and steep wooded hillsides in northern New Castle County. Its 28 roads form a network between Routes 52 and 48, rather than a single through road. DelDOT gives its length as approximately 27 miles and its driving time as about an hour. The department highlights the valley's natural areas and surviving evidence of grist, snuff and paper milling at Yorklyn.

These roads carried horse-and-buggy traffic before becoming a scenic network. The Delaware Nature Society and its partners nominated the byway in July 2004; it became a Delaware Scenic and Historic Highway on April 5, 2005. The valley's older transport history includes the Wilmington and Western Railroad, which opened to Landenberg in 1872. Historic Red Clay Valley, Inc. began weekend steam excursions in 1966, reviving the old railroad name. Floods in 1999 and 2003 destroyed timber trestles; the railroad replaced the lost bridges with steel.

The stops here begin at Ashland's covered bridge on Barley Mill Road beside the nature center. At Yorklyn, Auburn Valley State Park preserves the Marshall family estate and portions of its creekside mills. Wooddale's covered crossing completes this selection, with a replacement bridge built after the flood of 2003.

moments.title: Ashland Covered Bridge
moments.text: Ashland's covered bridge carries Barley Mill Road over Red Clay Creek beside the Ashland Nature Center. Built about 1860, it uses the Town lattice truss design developed by Ithiel Town. In 1965, an engineering survey documented it as one of Delaware's last three surviving covered bridges. The bridge entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. Traffic has repeatedly damaged the structure: oversized trucks struck it in 2011 and 2014 after drivers ignored the signs, and a snowplow crashed in 2017. High water and debris during Hurricane Ida damaged the covered span in 2021, prompting another temporary repair closure.

moments.title: Auburn Valley State Park
moments.text: Steam power links the Marshall family's mills with the cars preserved at Auburn Valley State Park. T. Clarence Marshall became a Stanley dealer and collected steam automobiles; the collection opened to the public in the 1970s. Volunteers maintain the vehicles in working order in the Auburn Heights carriage house. The collection includes 15 Stanley cars and a one-eighth-size steam locomotive that runs on tracks encircling the estate. Tom Marshall donated the collection in 2008; the nonprofit Friends of Auburn Heights Preserve owns it and works with the state. Above the mills and Yorklyn stands the Victorian mansion Israel Marshall built in 1897.

moments.title: Wooddale Bridge
moments.text: Wooddale's covered bridge is a replacement for a crossing built about 1850. Tropical Storm Henri destroyed the original in 2003, and DelDOT rebuilt it in 2007–08 with changes intended to resist future floods. The replacement used Bongossi wood; the roadway rose five feet, and the openings were enlarged. It reopened on December 15, 2008. Like Ashland, Wooddale uses Ithiel Town's lattice truss design. The two crossings remain from the thirteen bridges marked along Red Clay Creek on an 1868 map. The Town lattice span measures approximately 72 feet across Red Clay Creek.
